title: One-Line Rock Paper Scissors
tagline: A tiny Python game squeezed into two deliberately ridiculous lines
summary: This was a small code-golf experiment to see how much game logic I could compress without breaking it. The result fits the outcome logic on one line and the entire input loop on another. It is not the cleanest way to write a game, but finding the little Python tricks that made it possible was the whole point.

hero.alt: Black ink drawing of paper, rock, and scissors connected by arrows showing the winning cycle
hero.caption: The triangle behind the one-line win test: rock beats scissors, scissors beats paper, and paper beats rock.

sections.heading: The two lines
body: The game is a triangle rather than a straight ranking: rock beats scissors, scissors beats paper, and paper beats rock. The code turns that triangle into the numbered list [paper, rock, scissors], or [0, 1, 2]. Each choice beats the item one step ahead, with scissors wrapping from 2 back to paper at 0.

For paper and rock, adding one finds the choice they beat: 0 + 1 is rock, and 1 + 1 is scissors. Scissors is the wraparound case, so subtracting two turns its index 2 into paper's index 0. If neither test matches, equal indexes mean a tie and the remaining case is a loss.

Chained conditional expressions select the result text, while semicolons keep the input and output loop on one physical line. It is intentionally compressed code, but the triangle is the simple idea underneath it.
